Reading across vocabularies

Related terms, different claims.

Encrypted / cryptic / latent peptide
A potentially active sequence within a larger protein. The literature varies in whether the term requires demonstrated natural release, activity of a synthesized fragment, or only a prediction.
Cryptide
A functional cryptic peptide derived from a protein. Narrow usage emphasizes a fragment with an activity distinct from its parent; broader usage can include classical precursor-derived peptides.
Precursor-derived hormone
A mature signal produced by processing a larger precursor, such as insulin from proinsulin. This is a central historical connection, with a biosynthetic role that differs from incidental turnover of a multifunctional protein.
Endogenous peptide
A peptide present in the biological system being sampled. Detection establishes presence under the sampling conditions; it does not by itself establish a biological function or exclude processing during sample handling.
Peptidomics / degradomics / terminomics
Peptidomics profiles peptide populations. Proteolytic degradomics examines proteases, substrates and cleavage products. Terminomics enriches or maps protein and peptide termini to reveal processing events.
Adjacent discoveries
MHC ligands, small-ORF translation and engineered peptides contribute methods and concepts. Their inclusion here preserves these connections while distinguishing them from naturally released functional cryptides.

Terminology can be explored through the “Concepts & terminology” filter and the original papers linked in each entry. These definitions are editorial guides to the timeline, not claims of universal nomenclature.

Scope, provenance & reuse

A connected literature history.

How the atlas was assembled

Four parallel research streams covered early digestion and hormones; cryptides, food and host defense; degradation and analytical methods; and computational discovery through 2026. Searches combined peptide names, terminology variants, techniques and publication eras, then followed references to original reports. Follow-up searches expanded named experimental lineages, infection and immunomodulation, and evolutionary analyses. Additional parallel searches covered neuroactive and metabolic peptides, tissue remodeling and cancer, food and nutrition, proteostasis, biomarkers, and analytical and computational methods. A subsequent author-led pass followed verified coauthor lists backwards and forwards, checked related contributions against original studies, and removed duplicate papers. A deeper host-defense pass examined peptide-family discoveries and native-function experiments, chemokine and neuroendocrine fragments, immune-cell signaling and repair, infection and inflammation peptidomes, microbial resistance, computational design and clinical trials. It retained negative and qualifying experiments alongside positive findings and checked existing studies for missed immune scope. User-supplied sepsis reviews were used to trace additional primary studies of endotoxin neutralization, human immune measurements and clinical development; the reviews themselves remain labeled as literature syntheses. Review-led follow-up traced cryptome, latent-peptide, peptidomics and mining bibliographies to original papers, including oxygen-carrier and chromosomal cryptides, matrix and coagulation fragments, plant defense, milk and infection peptide pools, and large-scale analytical workflows. The flow marks large-scale peptidomics explicitly. Review-reference trails appear in study details where recorded and are retained in the downloadable data. Each study now has explicit labels for biological topics, reported techniques and biological systems. These labels drive the flow, map and combined filters. The host-defense focus starts with Hirsch’s 1956 phagocytin work and includes antimicrobial and immunomodulatory peptide research and host-defense-related peptidome studies in infection or inflammation. MHC antigen presentation and immunopeptidomics remain in the broader history, outside the host-defense view. A scope rationale distinguishes peptide-function and discovery studies from immune-context profiling and optional enabling methods. Labels describe the available study record; methods and systems that are not established are marked as unspecified. Topic membership does not establish physiological function.

Entries prioritize original research, method and database papers. Concept-defining reviews and essays are included as historical contributions and identified where appropriate. Historical archives support early foundations. Dates follow the reported discovery or publication event; online and issue dates are distinguished where verified.

The milestone count describes this curated selection, not the size or rate of research in the field. The histogram is a navigation aid and is not a bibliometric analysis.

What the evidence labels mean

“Experimental activity” includes biochemical, cellular and pharmacological tests of isolated or synthesized peptides. “Endogenous detection” indicates measurement in biological samples. “In vivo / physiological” identifies entries with organismal or endogenous-system evidence; the description specifies what was demonstrated. These are descriptive labels, not a universal ranking.

Sequence occurrence, natural production, biological activity and physiological necessity are separate questions. Source details retain distinctions between predicted candidates, experimentally tested subsets and engineered derivatives.

This is a broad, source-linked research atlas rather than a completed systematic review. Coverage is selective within very large subfields; early non-English archives, every peptide family, all food hydrolysates, clinical development and all recent preprints remain areas for expansion. Searches were completed on 13 October 2026.
